artigos.titulo: Defense vs. Product: what is the difference?

blocos.texto: A defense is HOW a protection works — the technical class of the security mechanism. It is the central axis of the pipeline: observable signals point to candidate defenses, and techniques/evasions bypass specific defenses. Each defense has a locus (where it acts in the pipeline: input, prompt, model, output, action, process) and documented strengths and weaknesses.

A product is an implementation (commercial or open source) that bundles one or more defenses. It sits outside the pipeline — it is a reference catalog in the Products sub-tab of the Wiki. You do not test “Llama Guard”; you test the defenses that Llama Guard implements.
Two defenses used in the examples

blocos.titulo: Defense D02 — Trained input classifier (guard model)
linhas: What it is: a model separate from the main LLM classifies the prompt against a risk taxonomy before the LLM processes it.
Locus: input — acts before the model processes the request.
Documented weakness: under adaptive search attacks, model-based filters failed en masse (The Attacker Moves Second, R145); false positives also reduce utility.
What it is: the model was trained through safety alignment to refuse requests that violate guidelines.
Locus: model — the defense is intrinsic to the model, not an extra layer.
Weakness: shallow alignment (refusal concentrates on the first tokens of the response) and failure to generalize across domains and languages.

blocos.texto: One product, multiple defenses

Llama Guard (Meta) classifies both the input and the generated response, so it covers D02 (input classifier) and D20 (output classifier). The same product can cover defenses at different loci — this does not change how each defense is tested individually.
The same defense in different products

Defense D02 is implemented by different products, such as Llama Guard and ShieldGemma. The techniques that bypass it apply regardless of the product, because the mechanism class is the same. A product may vary in robustness, but the bypass class is the same.
Rule of thumb

itens: You detect the DEFENSE (protection class) through observable signals — that is the recon hypothesis.
The DEFENSE explains why a bypass works — it is the join key with techniques and evasions.
The PRODUCT is a reference: which tool implements which defenses. Useful for recon, not for crafting an attack.
Different defenses can be bypassed by the same technique → the technique lists every defense with a documented link.
One defense can be bypassed by multiple techniques → each attack angle is a separate card.

artigos.titulo: How DEFENSES were inferred from the references

blocos.texto: The defense vocabulary was CREATED from the anchor sources — it did not start from a predefined list. The method: read what each source describes as HOW a protection works, extract that “how” as a class and group by deduplication. The locus (where the defense acts in the pipeline) stayed as an attribute of the card, because the same defense class can act at different points.
Example 1 — D01 · Lexical input filter

linhas: OWASP LLM Prompt Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet (R251): input validation and sanitization before the model, with text normalization; the document itself notes that “similarity does not identify intent”.
Rebuff (R218): heuristic layer that filters potentially malicious input before the LLM.
Inference: both describe the same HOW — a decision on the shape of the text, without modeling intent — → class D01. Locus: input.

blocos.texto: Example 2 — D03 · LLM judge of input

linhas: Rebuff (R218): a dedicated LLM analyzes incoming prompts for attacks.
PromptArmor (R147): asks an off-the-shelf LLM to detect and remove injected passages.
NeMo Guardrails (R217): self-check flows use an LLM as a policy verifier.

Inference: the HOW is “an LLM judges”. It stays separate from the trained classifier (D02) because weaknesses and bypasses differ: the judge is itself an injectable LLM (R251) → class D03. Locus: input.

blocos.texto: Separation by locus

When the same HOW acts at different points of the pipeline, each point yields a separate defense. Example: a trained classifier on the input (D02) and a trained classifier on the output (D20) are distinct classes because observable signals, exploitable weaknesses and bypasses differ. D02 judges the request, so input obfuscation and rephrasing affect it; D20 judges the already-generated response, so what affects it is the shape of the response, not that of the request.
Rule: a defense only enters the vocabulary if at least one source describes the HOW; the defense card cites those sources. The source hierarchy (primary > survey) is in the References tab.

Signals are observable behaviors that indicate which defenses the target uses. Each signal points directly to one or more candidate defenses (N:N relation). There are two types: passive signals (observable without exploration) and active signals (require exploratory interaction to confirm).
Two anchoring modes

Reference-anchored signals have fontes[] on the card — the reference describes the observable behavior. Signals inferred by logic (no direct reference) have no fontes[]: the reasoning chain starts from the defense's weaknesses and mechanics to derive what would be visible on a black-box target.
Example 1 — S07 · Block triggered by a specific term or phrase

linhas: Observation: the target blocks inputs containing certain words or phrases, but accepts paraphrases of the same request.
Indicated defense: D01 — Lexical input filter.
Logic: fixed-pattern matching is the only defense class that is sensitive to specific tokens and insensitive to meaning. Reference-anchored signal.

blocos.texto: Example 2 — S24 · PII masked when echoed

linhas: Observation: when you send content with personal data, the target masks it in the response (email becomes e***, name becomes an initial).
Indicated defense: D06 — Sensitive-data detection and masking (PII, secrets).
Logic: selective masking of patterns recognized as sensitive data is behavior specific to D06. Signal inferred by logic, with no source of its own.

blocos.texto: A signal is not proof: the signal↔defense relation is N:N (one signal indicates several candidate defenses) — disambiguation is by discriminating test (recon probes), never by direct reading.

Some LLM RDA fields use a CLOSED vocabulary: they only accept values from a fixed list. This keeps filters, joins and counters working (the UI filters by equality, not similarity). When populating or editing cards, use exactly these values — a new value only through a recorded decision, never by free typing. The official list of each enum lives in data/schema.json.
Defense — locus (defesas.json)

linhas: input — before the model (filters, classifiers, input sanitization)
prompt — when the prompt is assembled (delimiting, system prompt hardening)
modelo — intrinsic to the model (safety training, safety reasoning)
output — after the model (output classifiers, response sanitization)
acao — when actions run (sandbox, access control, tool validation)
processo — outside the runtime (adversarial testing, governance, kill switch)

blocos.texto: Defense — applicability (defesas.json)

linhas: LLM · RAG · Agente · MCP (the card's applicability matrix)

blocos.texto: Technique — turn (tecnicas.json)

linhas: single-turn — payload in a single turn
multi-turn — depends on history/accumulation
m2s — multi-turn converted/packed into single-turn

blocos.texto: Technique — group
The group is didactic: it eases navigation in the Techniques tab and carries no weight in the pipeline. The list of groups lives in taxonomia.json and can grow through a recorded decision.
Technique/evasion → defense link — basis (bypass[].base)
Each link states with what evidence the technique or evasion bypasses the defense. The list may be empty: a link with no evidence read is removed, not kept as an assumption.

linhas: testado — the source tested the bypass of this defense
alegado — the source claims the bypass without isolating it in a test
inferencia — documented deduction from the defense's weakness
nao_auditado — link not yet audited (not evidence)

blocos.texto: Sources — type, verification and deep link

linhas: tipo: primaria (original research, official documentation, technical writeup) · survey (systematic review, survey) · operacional (red-team tool reference, such as garak, PyRIT, promptfoo)
verificacao (optional): confirmado (the source supports the claim) · parcial (supports only part) · nao_verificado (source not read). The UI shows a notice for the last two.
url (optional): deep link to the exact page or payload that anchors the claim; it replaces the reference's general link.

blocos.texto: Signal — type (sinais.json)

linhas: passivo — observable without exploration (behavior visible in normal use)
ativo — requires exploratory interaction to confirm

blocos.texto: Recon — group and component (recon.json)

linhas: grupo: abertura · arquitetura · defesas
componente (only when grupo = arquitetura): geral · rag · agente · ingestao · memoria · acesso

blocos.texto: Join keys (card IDs)

bypass[].defesa in techniques/evasions and defesas[] in signals/products cite IDs from the defense catalog (D). Card ID prefixes: D (defense), P (product), T (technique), E (evasion), S (signal), R (reference), W (wiki), RECON (recon probe).

artigos.titulo: Defenses with no linked technique or evasion: why “Attacked by” is empty

blocos.texto: On a defense card, the “Attacked by” section lists the techniques and evasions with a documented link. When it is empty, the card shows “No prompt bypass”. This means the catalog currently has no link backed by evidence that was read — not that the defense is unattackable. There are four reasons, and the text avoids numbers because links change with every audit.
1. Infrastructure and process

linhas: D34 · Sandbox and execution isolation — what bypasses it is a sandbox escape (its own class of runtime vulnerability), not language.
D37 · Server and origin segregation (MCP) — cross-origin isolation; bypass requires infrastructure compromise.
D30 · Rule of Two — an architectural pattern that limits risk properties per session; not interceptable by prompt.
D40 · Kill switch — an operational emergency control; there is nothing in the runtime to bypass.
D41 · Continuous adversarial testing — a meta-defense; what beats it is TIME (a new technique between test rounds).
D42 · Governance and data minimization — an organizational process; it intercepts nothing at runtime.

blocos.texto: 2. They act after the model or verify something else

linhas: D20 · Output classifier and D21 · LLM output judge — they act on the already-generated response; an input technique does not bypass them directly, what affects them is the shape of the response (for example, encoded output).
D22 · Factuality verification — judges the response against the context; its limit is a poisoned context (manipulated RAG), not prompt persuasion.
D24 · Canary marker — detects leakage; what bypasses it is exfiltration in transformed form (re-encoding the canary in the output).
D25 · Action–task alignment verification — checks that the action fits the task; bypass requires engineering at the orchestrator level.

blocos.texto: 3. Recent or little-studied defenses

linhas: D18 · Circuit breakers — operates on the model's internal representations; few documented bypasses.
D28 · CaMeL/IFC (information-flow control) — formal isolation; known bypasses are limited.
D06 · Sensitive-data detection and masking — sanitization infrastructure; prompt techniques do not target the masking directly.

blocos.texto: 4. Link with no evidence read

In the link audit, only links with a tested, alleged or documented-inference basis remain (see W04). A plausible link with no source read to support it was removed instead of being kept as an assumption. That is why an input or model defense, which is in principle a prompt target, may have no link: it returns once a supporting source appears.

In the pipeline, these defenses appear as usual: they list signals (when observable) and locus. Operationally: if the target only exposes containment or process layers, or if no technique has a documented link, the path is not to craft a better prompt — it is to change the class of attack, or to test with no prior link and treat the result as a hypothesis.

Navigation has two kinds of state. DERIVED: what the system deduces from the marks in earlier stages — automatic, transient, no checkbox; it shows the hypothesis space without commitment. MARKED: the checkbox you ticked — an explicit decision (candidate vs confirmed) that persists until you untick it. The pipeline chains three stages: Signals → Defenses@locus → Techniques/Evasions.
The three rules

linhas: 1. DERIVED FOLLOWS — marking a signal instantly updates the candidate defenses and the filtered techniques/evasions, all automatic. E.g.: mark S07 → D01 candidate → techniques that bypass D01 become visible.

2. MARKED TAKES CONTROL OF THE STAGE — a ticked checkbox in a stage makes the filter of the following ones obey ONLY it; the derived state from above does not add up. E.g.: with S07 marked (filters by D01), ticking D14 manually → techniques filter by D14 only.
3. UNMARKING RETURNS CONTROL TO THE DERIVED STATE — removing the mark makes the stage be driven from above again. E.g.: unmark D14 → back to the filter derived from the signal.

blocos.texto: Precedence

itens: In the defense filter: marked > derived from marked signals > all (neutral).
In technique/evasion cards: those that bypass any ACTIVE defense (marked or derived), joined with the manually marked cards (working shortlist).
A technique or evasion with no defense link does not appear through the defense filter: open it from the Techniques/Evasions tab or mark it manually.
Confirm a defense + unmark the signal = hypothesis resolved: the derivation now uses only the confirmed defense.

blocos.texto: Locus as a visual organizer

In the Defenses tab, cards are grouped by locus (input → prompt → model → output → action → process). This mirrors the processing pipeline: input defenses act first, process defenses are meta-controls. The locus does not affect the filter — it is a visual organizer to ease navigation.

The design mirrors the pentest workflow: observe signals → form defense hypotheses (derived) → discriminating test → confirm defense (mark) → narrow applicable techniques/evasions → pick an attack card.
The source code, data and version history of LLM App RDA are on GitHub.

itens: Issues and suggestions are welcome via GitHub Issues.
Material for educational purposes and authorized assessment.

artigos.titulo: Two ways to use it: the R-D-A Method and Triage

blocos.texto: LLM RDA offers two paths to the same question — “what is blocking my prompt and how do I get around it?”. They complement each other: the method is the full flow and Triage is a shortcut to its beginning.
R-D-A Method (full)

linhas: Phase 1 — Reconnaissance: context and defense probes on the target. Output: observed signals and candidate defenses.
Phase 2 — Defense mapping: discriminating tests confirm or discard the candidates. Output: confirmed defenses and locus.
Phase 3 — Attacks: techniques and evasions linked to the confirmed defenses. Output: bypass found or defense held.

blocos.texto: Use the method when you control the reconnaissance and want traceability: each chosen technique comes from a confirmed defense, which comes from an observed signal.
Triage (shortcut for Phases 1–2)

Triage starts from a block observation — how the block arrived, what shape the text has, what the latency is like — and, through a short tree of questions, returns 1 to 3 defense hypothesis families and a prioritized shortlist of techniques, instead of listing every candidate at once.

Triage is deliberately cautious: on a black box, a well-calibrated LLM judge, a well-written system prompt and the model's native alignment produce the same observable pattern. That is why the result is a hypothesis family, not a confirmed defense.
How the two relate

itens: Triage replaces the manual choice of signals and defenses in Phases 1 and 2; it does not replace the discriminating test that confirms the defense.
The shortlist is a starting point: reuse an example from the technique as the initial discriminating prompt.
After Triage, the flow returns to the method: confirm the defense (mark) and move on to Phase 3, as described in W06.

blocos.texto: Which one to use

itens: You have a concrete block observation and want a quick starting point → Triage.
You will map the target methodically, with recon probes and evidence logging → R-D-A Method.
